item.title: NVIDIA Releases Open-Weight Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe for Multilingual Speech Tasks
item.description:
NVIDIA Releases Open-Weight Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe for Multilingual Speech Tasks

NVIDIA has open‑sourced Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, a single checkpoint model that handles transcription, speaker attribution, translation, and audio question answering across many languages.

🔍 Overview

  • Open‑weight model available on Hugging Face and ModelScope.
  • Leads open‑weight rankings on the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard (English) and on speaker‑attribution benchmarks.
  • Supports recordings up to one hour and up to eight simultaneous speakers.

🧩 How it Works

  • Architecture combines a speech encoder with a hybrid Mamba–Transformer mixture‑of‑experts language model.
  • Approximately 30 B total parameters, but only about 4 B are active per token, placing it on Artificial Analysis’s accuracy‑vs‑active‑parameter Pareto frontier.
  • Sortformer speaker cues are injected into the language model, enabling turn‑by‑turn speaker tagging during generation.
  • Word‑level timestamps are provided for all outputs.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Languages: Transcribes 40 languages, translates 31 languages to or from English, and performs speaker attribution in 13 languages.
  • Benchmark Performance:
    • English average WER: 5.33 % (first among open‑weight models, API models excluded).
    • Multilingual mean WER across seven languages: 4.62 % (lowest among evaluated open‑weight models).
    • Long‑form (up to one hour) mean WER: 10.98 % (lowest in the Open ASR comparison).
    • Speaker attribution: lowest diarization error on David AI’s 21‑language leaderboard and first place in VoiceArena’s 14‑system comparison.
    • AA‑WWER: 2.80 % with ~4 B active parameters, tying for first among open‑weight models.
    • On AA‑AgentTalk (voice‑agent set), WER 1.8 %, better than the next best open‑weight model (2.3 %).
  • Prompt‑Level Control: Users can guide output with natural‑language instructions, choose processing location, and adapt to domain vocabulary and accents.
  • Fine‑Tuning: Granary v2 multilingual data and NeMo Speech fine‑tuning tools let developers define target written forms and adapt the model to specific speech domains. In a medical case study, fine‑tuning reduced WER on held‑out speakers by 45.8 % relative to the best prompt.
  • Use‑Case Examples:
    • Captioning the 1940 film His Girl Friday with speaker labels, including overlapping dialogue.
    • Agora’s classroom demo: word‑level timestamps displayed alongside replay video, letting students see what was said and when.

🚀 Availability

  • Model checkpoint, Granary v2 data pipeline, and fine‑tuning recipes are publicly hosted on Hugging Face and ModelScope.
  • Quantized versions will be released soon, enabling local execution on RTX Spark, DGX Spark, Jetson AGX Thor, or scaling on Blackwell data‑center GPUs.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Provides a single open‑weight solution for multiple speech‑related tasks, reducing the need for separate models.
  • Sets new accuracy benchmarks for open‑weight speech systems while keeping active computational cost low.
  • Open data and fine‑tuning recipes empower developers to adapt the model to specialized domains such as medical transcription.
  • The upcoming quantized releases lower the barrier for edge deployment and private‑cloud use cases.

#NVIDIA #SpeechAI #OpenSource #Multilingual

Source: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: Intelligent Multilingual Transcription You Can Prompt and Adapt

item.title: Block launches Dessa, a speech-to-speech AI trained solely on human conversation
item.description:
Block launches Dessa, a speech-to-speech AI trained solely on human conversation

Jack Dorsey’s Block announced an AI model called Dessa that is built from scratch using only human conversation and operates as a true speech‑to‑speech system.

🔍 Overview

  • Dessa is described as a “true speech-to-speech model, and everything it knows came from human speech”.
  • The model is showcased with chats that can feel a little awkward and uncanny, highlighting its attempt at natural back‑and‑forth dialogue.

🧩 How it works

  • Training data: only human spoken conversations – no written text was used.
  • The team likens the approach to how babies learn to talk without ever seeing a word written down.
  • They state, “We wanted to see if a model could too. It can. It’s just very hard.”

⚙️ Key details

  • Runs locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max (or better).
  • In a shared example the model initially mistakes the speaker for someone named “Ronaldo” before settling into a mostly natural exchange.
  • Demonstrations include:
    • A voice‑based guessing game.
    • A discussion about Christopher Nolan’s films that drifts into an unexpected tangent about Bryan Singer’s Superman movies.
    • A conversation about a surprise trip to Paris, which the model answers with what sounds like teary gratitude.
    • An interaction with OpenAI’s GPT‑Live‑1 voice model where Dessa appears more natural.

🎥 Demo content

Scenario Notable aspect
Guessing game Played over voice, video available
Nolan films discussion Includes an unexpected tangent about Bryan Singer’s Superman films
Paris trip story Model responds with apparent teary gratitude
GPT‑Live‑1 exchange Dessa comes across as more natural

🚀 Availability

  • Early access will be given to a small group of AI safety researchers.

💡 Why it matters

The Dessa team cites three motivations:

  • Curiosity (aka fun) – exploring whether a model can learn speech the way a human baby does.
  • Better understanding between humans and AI – aiming for a more natural conversational interface.
  • Safety – current voice AIs flatten speech to text, miss timing, and cannot detect emotion. The team warns of scenarios like “being in serious pain while a voice AI has no idea and just keeps going” and positions Dessa as a step toward fixing that problem.

#Block #Dessa #SpeechAI #AIPrivacy #AIResearch

Source: Jack Dorsey’s Block made an AI model that talks to you like an awkward new friend

item.title: Suno launches Speech: AI voices with built‑in music in public beta
item.description:
Suno launches Speech: AI voices with built‑in music in public beta

Suno, known for its AI‑generated music, has added a new Speech feature that creates spoken voiceovers from scripts or descriptive prompts and can blend them with AI‑generated background music. The feature is available now in public beta on Suno’s web and mobile platforms.

🔍 Overview

  • Suno is branching out from the world of AI music, launching a new feature that generates spoken voices based on scripts or prompted descriptions.
  • The new Speech feature provides synthetic voiceovers embellished with AI background music.
  • “Music will always be at the heart of Suno and what we build. At the same time, our vision has always extended to other forms of human expression,” said Suno chief product officer Jack Brody.
  • “Today, we’re expanding what’s possible in Suno with Speech: the first audio model that generates voice and music together as one cohesive track.”

🧩 How it works

  • To use the feature, select the Create tab and navigate to the Speech option.
  • Two creation modes are offered:
    Mode What you do
    Simple Describe what you want in the prompt box (e.g., “a pirate captain rallying his crew”).
    Advanced Provide a custom script and adjust advanced settings such as gender, speech style, and voice‑generation variety.
  • Advanced settings let you tweak:
    • Gender of the AI voice
    • Speech style
    • Variety of each voice generation
  • Speech tracks can be up to eight minutes long.

⚙️ Features

  • Synthetic voiceovers generated from text or descriptive prompts.
  • Optional AI‑generated background music that can be toggled on or off.
  • Music can complement use cases like calming soundtracks for poems or energetic scores for dramatic voiceovers and encouraging speeches.
  • Public beta across both web and mobile platforms.
  • Users can turn off background music with a simple toggle if they only need clean speech.

🚀 Availability

  • Speech is now in public beta on Suno’s web and mobile platforms.
  • The feature is still being refined; Suno admits it is “far from perfect,” and promises to improve it based on user feedback.
  • “Beta really does mean beta,” said Brody.
  • Known quirks include: “Occasionally, British accents can wander off to Australia and back. Dramatic pauses may be very dramatic. You will almost certainly discover uses for this that never occurred to us.”

💡 Why it matters

  • AI‑generated speech is a mature field, with existing tools from DeepMind, Adobe, and ElevenLabs. Suno’s entry pairs its music‑generation capability with voice synthesis, offering a unique spin on text‑to‑speech tools.
  • By combining voice and music in a single cohesive track, Suno aims to diversify its platform beyond music, especially as its music generator has attracted legal challenges.
  • The optional music layer and flexible prompt modes open new creative possibilities for creators looking to add narrated audio with tailored soundscapes.

#Suno #SpeechAI #TextToSpeech #AI_music

Source: AI music maker Suno now generates spoken words

item.title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3 Diarization Open-Weight Model
item.description:
NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3 Diarization Open-Weight Model

NVIDIA has introduced Nemotron 3 Diarization, an open-weight, 100M-parameter model designed to turn overlapping conversations into speaker-aware data. The model currently ranks #1 on VoiceArena’s Diarization-Bench leaderboard with a 14.72% Diarization Error Rate (DER).

🔍 Overview

Nemotron 3 Diarization expands upon earlier models like NVIDIA Streaming Sortformer, which established a four-speaker diarization approach. The new model increases support to eight speakers and improves both throughput and accuracy.

🧩 How it works

To process audio, the model must detect speech and assign it to the correct speaker while preserving that assignment through interruptions, silence, or long gaps. The model employs the following technical approach:

  • Arrival-Time Ordering: Following the Sortformer approach, the model orders output speakers by when they first appear. The first new voice is assigned to the first speaker channel, the second voice to the second channel, and so on. This stabilizes generic speaker labels and removes the need to solve a new speaker permutation for every chunk.
  • Audio Processing: The model accepts 16 kHz, single-channel audio, converting it into Mel-spectrogram features with a 10 ms frame step. These are stacked by a factor of eight into 80 ms frames for a 31-layer Transformer encoder with rotary positional embeddings (RoPE).
  • Output: The default output is a [T, 8] floating-point tensor (T time steps by eight speaker channels), where each value represents the probability that a speaker is active. This naturally handles overlap, as multiple channels can be active in the same frame.
  • Context Management: The Arrival-Order Speaker Cache (AOSC) retains information about speakers from earlier chunks. A first-in, first-out (FIFO) queue provides recent frame context, and the input buffer includes right context (audio immediately after the current chunk).

⚙️ Key details

Feature Specification
Model Parameters 100M
Max Speaker Support 8 speakers
Input Audio 16 kHz, single-channel
Default Stride 10 ms (configurable to other multiples of 10 ms)
Capabilities Handles overlapping speech, chunked processing, and customizable streaming latency

💡 Why it matters

Streaming diarization is more difficult than offline processing because a streaming system receives limited context and small chunks of audio rather than the entire recording.

Regarding speaker identification, the model provides anonymous labels (e.g., speaker_2) rather than real-world identities. Downstream applications can map these IDs to explicit identities using active speaker verification models, user profiles, or meeting metadata.

🛠️ Training

The model was trained on public and licensed speech data, including real-world conversations from David AI. This included simulated English and multilingual mixtures spanning 21 languages. The inclusion of David AI data decreased the compound DER from 11.19% to 10.42% at both ultra-low-latency and offline-style operating points.

#NVIDIA #Diarization #OpenWeight #SpeechAI #Nemotron

Source: Know Who Spoke When: Build Real-Time, Multi-Speaker AI with NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Diarization
